stories.headline: GOLDMAN PUSHES FED CUTS TO 2027 AS MAY PAYROLLS CRUSH EXPECTATIONS
stories.body: The U.S. added 172,000 jobs in May vs. an 85,000 consensus estimate, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.3%. Goldman Sachs now forecasts no Fed rate cuts until 2027, projecting core PCE above 3% through year-end; markets now price a 72% chance of a December rate hike — the highest probability since 2023.
stories.explain: 172K vs. an 85K estimate isn't just a beat — it's nearly double consensus, which wipes out the 'weakening labor market' narrative the Fed would need to justify any cut. Goldman had been calling for two 2026 cuts as recently as March; one jobs print reversed that entirely, and December rate-hike odds jumped to 72% — the highest since 2023. The Fed's dual mandate is now one-sided: employment is at 4.3%, so inflation is the only variable left, and a tight labor market means wage pressure isn't going anywhere.

stories.headline: IRAN-ISRAEL EXCHANGE WEEKEND STRIKES; WTI SURGES ABOVE $93
stories.body: Iran and Israel traded missile strikes for the first time since April's ceasefire, threatening President Trump's 60-day truce efforts. Continued near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted Persian Gulf supply; WTI crude jumped 4.2% to $93.60 and Brent topped $94, adding fresh inflationary pressure to an already hawkish Fed backdrop.
stories.explain: What makes this exchange hit harder than baseline Iran-Israel tension is the ceasefire context — April's truce had already been priced in as a de-escalation, so re-escalation now reprices the entire probability distribution of a prolonged conflict. Markets aren't reacting to one strike; they're reacting to the signal that the 60-day truce is failing. The $93.60 WTI print is particularly painful because it lands the same week as Wednesday's CPI — higher energy costs feed directly into headline inflation, giving the Fed one more reason to stay hawkish.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS POWER S&P REBOUND; BITCOIN RECLAIMS $63K AHEAD OF CPI
stories.body: The S&P 500 gained 0.8% and Nasdaq 100 surged 1.5% Monday, led by semiconductor names bouncing from last week's rate-shock selloff. Bitcoin climbed back above $63,000 after May saw $2.4B in net ETF outflows — the largest monthly drawdown since November 2025. Wednesday's CPI print is the week's defining catalyst.
stories.explain: Last week's rate-shock session took the Nasdaq down ~4.5% in a single day, so Monday's 1.5% bounce looks like a recovery — but it's a relief rally into Wednesday's CPI, not a fundamental re-rating. If CPI prints hot, the same rate-hike logic that triggered last week's selloff reasserts immediately. Bitcoin's $2.4B May ETF outflow — the largest monthly drawdown since November 2025 — matters because it signals institutional de-risking, not retail panic selling; that money doesn't come back fast, which is why the $63K reclaim is fragile.

stories.headline: GOLD AT TWO-MONTH LOW AS RATE-HIKE ODDS SURGE; ECB MEETS THURSDAY
stories.body: Gold slid to a two-month low near $4,314 as the stronger dollar (DXY 100.11) and surging rate expectations weighed on precious metals. Thursday brings the ECB rate decision alongside U.S. PPI and weekly jobless claims — a trifecta that could set the tone for risk assets heading into summer.
stories.explain: Here's the paradox: Iran-Israel missile strikes are exactly the kind of geopolitical shock that normally sends gold higher as a safe-haven. But gold is down today anyway. DXY at 100.11 (a strong-dollar level not seen during most of 2025) makes gold more expensive for foreign buyers, suppressing demand globally. More importantly, with December rate-hike odds at 72%, a 5.25% Treasury yields real income — gold yields nothing. When real rates are this elevated, the fear premium from a Middle East conflict simply isn't enough to offset the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.

stories.headline: NCAA PROPOSES NEW AGE-BASED ELIGIBILITY CLOCK; VOTE EXPECTED BY MONTH END
stories.body: The Division I Cabinet modified its age-based eligibility proposal, starting athletes' clocks at full-time enrollment or the academic year following their 19th birthday, whichever is sooner. The revision addresses concerns from men's basketball, ice hockey, and service academies; a final vote is expected before June 30.

stories.headline: KNICKS LEAD FINALS 2-0; GAME 3 TONIGHT AT MADISON SQUARE GARDEN
stories.body: New York's 13-game postseason winning streak is second-longest in NBA history, trailing only the 1998-99 Spurs. Game 2 drew 16.93M viewers on ABC, up 90% from last year's Game 1. The Spurs face historic pressure — no team has rallied from 0-2 in the Finals without winning Game 3. Tip-off 8:30 PM ET.

stories.headline: MANDATORY MINICAMP OPENS ACROSS NFL; PENIX KNEE RECOVERY ON TRACK
stories.body: All 32 teams begin mandatory minicamp this week. Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr. is hitting every rehab milestone but coach Kevin Stefanski gave a 'we'll see' on 11-on-11 clearance. Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett is attending to avoid fines while seeking a new contract after skipping voluntary workouts.

stories.headline: COURT RESTORES TEXAS TECH QB SORSBY'S ELIGIBILITY FOR 2026 SEASON
stories.body: A district court in Lubbock County granted an injunction allowing Brendan Sorsby to play in 2026, ruling he would face 'probable, imminent and irreparable injury' without relief. The ruling is the latest in a wave of eligibility litigation reshaping the NCAA landscape ahead of the 12-team CFP's third season.

deepDive.title: The Fed's Reaction Function: Why a Strong Jobs Report Can Hit Stocks Like a Rate Hike
content: Friday's May payrolls print — +172,000 vs. an 85,000 consensus — wasn't just a beat; it was a thesis-killer. Goldman Sachs, which had been forecasting multiple Fed cuts in 2026, pushed its timeline out to 2027 overnight. Rate-hike odds for December surged to 72%. Gold fell to a two-month low. The Nasdaq 100 lost nearly 4.5% in a single session. That kind of market response to a 'good' economic number only makes sense once you understand how the Fed's reaction function actually works.

The Fed targets two things simultaneously: maximum employment and price stability (2% inflation). When both objectives are in tension — strong jobs but sticky inflation — the Fed must choose. In mid-2026, that choice is stark: the labor market is robust (4.3% unemployment, solid wage growth), but core PCE remains above 3%. The Taylor Rule — a formula linking the policy rate to inflation and output gaps — would currently suggest a federal funds rate above 5.5%. With the effective rate at roughly 5.25%, the Fed is already behind the rule's prescription. A 172K print tightens labor further and removes any urgency to cut — or raises the case to hike.

This dynamic — strong growth tightening financial conditions through rate expectations — is sometimes called the 'good news is bad news' regime. It's not new: markets traded in this mode for most of 2022–23 as the Fed hiked aggressively. What's notable now is how quickly the market re-entered it. As recently as March, consensus called for two 2026 cuts. The May jobs shock reversed that in one session. Real yields (the 10Y TIPS breakeven is now above 2.5%) are at multi-year highs, meaning the discount rate applied to every future corporate cash flow just ratcheted up. Tech and growth stocks — whose valuations depend most heavily on long-duration discounting — took the biggest hit.

Wednesday's CPI print is now the week's most important data release. Core CPI ran at +0.3% MoM in April; if May prints +0.4% or above, expect rate-hike odds to surge past 80% and growth stocks to retest last week's lows. A soft +0.2% read would provide partial relief and could reprice some 2026 cuts back in — but Goldman and JPMorgan have already structurally revised their Fed calls, so any rally may be capped. The 'super-core' reading (services ex-shelter ex-energy) is what the Fed watches most carefully; that's where sticky inflation actually lives, and a sustained above-trend print there would make a rate hike before year-end a near-certainty.
